target_customer: Hospitals, clinics and physicians treating recurrent C. difficile infection (cost passed through as processing and shipping fees), funded by philanthropy
problem: Patients with recurrent C. diff had few options and no safe, standardized access to fecal microbiota transplants, because finding, screening and processing donors was hard for individual clinicians.
business_model: Nonprofit stool bank charging cost-recovery fees per treatment, supported by grants and donations; since 2025 a foundation funding microbiome research
product_category: Nonprofit stool bank for fecal microbiota transplant (healthcare)

founders.name: Mark Smith
education: MIT, microbiology student at the time (Wikipedia)
founders.background_notes: Wikipedia names him and James Burgess as founders in 2012.

founders.name: James Burgess
education: MIT Sloan MBA student at the time (Wikipedia)

founders.name: Majdi Osman
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as co-founder and physician-scientist researching the microbiome.

technical_complexity.rationale: Donor screening, processing, quality control and frozen logistics under FDA enforcement discretion; operationally hard rather than technologically novel.

defensibility.rationale: Its position as the first public stool bank with standardized screening gave a trusted supply, but it depended on the FDA tolerating stool banks.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: FDA ended enforcement discretion for stool banks; OpenBiome stopped delivering treatments at the end of 2024 and became a foundation.

market_need_then: Recurrent C. diff had few treatment options and clinicians lacked safe, standardized FMT supply; OpenBiome delivered over 72,000 treatments to 1,300 hospitals and clinics over about a decade per its own page.

branding.domain_note: Uses openbiome.org per the company site.
branding.brand_signature: First public stool bank, widely covered with poop bank headlines

rebrands.why: Stopped delivering FMT after the FDA ended enforcement discretion for stool banks; now funds microbiome research

branding.community_and_virality: Press including MIT News, Gizmodo, Fox News and Science News covered the first stool bank and its donor program (headlines seen in search results).

brand_strength.rationale: Strong press attention as the first public stool bank, but no evidence of a brand driven community beyond mission recognition; no source explains the name.

pivots.from: Collecting, screening and shipping FMT material
pivots.to: Announced winding down the stool bank program (later disputed as a closure)
pivots.why: A yearlong COVID-19 pause caused financial strain per STAT; shipped just over 200 in 2020

pivots.to: OpenBiome Foundation funding microbiome research and advocacy
pivots.why: FDA ended enforcement discretion for stool banks

outcome_analysis: OpenBiome built the first public stool bank and shipped over 72,000 treatments to about 1,300 sites over roughly a decade, then lost its core service when the FDA ended enforcement discretion for stool banks, ending deliveries around the end of 2024. A 2020 COVID shutdown of shipping had already caused strain, and the organization is now a foundation, so a regulatory change rather than lack of demand ended the model.
notes: Nonprofit, so conventional rounds do not apply. The Kellen Foundation grant has no amount or date in the source seen. Founding year is 2012 per Wikipedia and its story page, 2013 per YC and its own timeline. Wikipedia and YC list different founders (Smith and Burgess versus Osman and Edelstein); all are recorded with sources. The STAT 2026 claim that FDA halted shipments at end of 2024 is from a search snippet only. Status Active in directory matches since the foundation continues. No competitor source dated near the March 2020 batch was opened (the one opened was December 2021), so the list is empty. Treatment counts: 72,000 per OpenBiome page, 70,000 as of February 2024 per Wikipedia.
